counties.heading: Who governs your county?
counties.intro: Under California Elections Code §9118, a petition signed by voters equal to 10% of the ballots cast for Governor forces your board of supervisors to adopt the ordinance as written or put it to the voters. Those are its only two options, and the number is smaller than you would guess.
counties.citeMosca: Mosca, 1896: a minority governs not because it is wiser or better born, but because it is organised against a majority that is not.

modes.shareHint: How large the requirement is next to the county's electorate.
modes.peopleHint: Signatures required, on a logarithmic scale, because the raw counts span four orders of magnitude.

rail.selectPrompt: Point at a county to see what it requires.
rail.sources: Secretary of State, Statement of Vote · Report of Registration · US Census. Every figure links to its record.

scale.heading: The county is not a convenience.
scale.body1: It is the smallest scale at which a decision binds and one person is not a rounding error. Statewide, an initiative statute needs {{statute}} signatures and a constitutional amendment {{amendment}}. Your share of that is arithmetic noise.
scale.body2: In your county the same right has a number small enough that you could name the people behind it. Nothing about it is secret: it is the ballots cast for Governor in 2022, divided by ten.
scale.cite: Tocqueville: local institutions are where citizens actually learn the practice of liberty. The county is not a design convenience.

fair.heading: The right already exists. That was never the problem.
fair.body1: Every citizen may petition, comment, show up, vote. Exercising those rights well takes time, research, and interpretive skill. Those are distributed about as evenly as wealth is, and a liberty you lack the resources to use is a liberty in name only.
fair.body2: So the public is not absent. It is eclipsed, unable to see easily which decisions reach it or trace who made them. That is not apathy, and it will not be fixed by telling anyone to care more.
fair.cite: Rawls on the fair value of political liberty; Dewey on the eclipse of the public.

cost.heading: So we changed the cost, not the citizen.
cost.body1: Handing the decision to experts has been tried for a century. So has exhorting people to pay closer attention. The remaining move is to lower what it costs to know, at the one scale where knowing still converts into anything.
cost.body2: It matters more than its size suggests. Almost every civic tool helps you answer a question somebody else decided to ask. A county initiative is one of the few places where the question itself is up for grabs.
cost.cite: Schattschneider: the decisive power is not the vote but the prior question of which alternatives get considered at all. The chorus of organised interests, he observed, sings with an upper-class accent.

items.ballotBody: Every measure, in plain language, next to the text it was drawn from, so you can check the summary against the thing itself.
items.moneyBody: Contributions and expenditures traced to the committee that filed them, not to whoever cut the cheque last.
items.decidesBody: Your representatives, the meetings where it happens, and how each of them voted.
items.doBody: The threshold for your county, and whether the petition someone just handed you is a real one.

check.heading: Do not take our word for any of it.
check.body1: A tool that asks for trust has recreated the problem it claims to solve. Every number here carries a link to the public record it came from: the Statement of Vote, the Report of Registration, the Census. If we are wrong, the source says so.
check.body2: The code is open. The prompts are published. Anything an AI wrote is labelled as such, and sits next to the record it was drawn from.
check.cite: Rawls: a liberty some citizens lack the resources to exercise is a liberty in name only, and its worth has to be guaranteed rather than asserted.

footnote.heading: The details that matter
footnote.statute: The 10% requirement is set by <0>California Elections Code §9118</0>. A petition at 20% compels a special election rather than waiting for the next regular one.
footnote.notPassing: Qualifying a measure is not passing one. These figures put a question to the voters; the voters decide it.
footnote.cities: Cities work differently: a general-law city sets its bar at 10% of registered voters rather than votes cast, and a charter city sets its own.
footnote.cycle: Figures reflect the November 2022 gubernatorial general and will change after November 2026.
